lesson.title: De & Het: Gender Without Case
lesson.subtitle: two articles, no noun case, and the compounds that decode them

hook.title: Two Articles, Not Three
hook.content: Dutch nouns are de (common) or het (neuter). There is no noun case system to learn: the article does not change when the noun is a subject or object. That already makes Dutch easier than German.

pattern.title: Read the word, not the meaning
pattern.content: De and het are lexical: tafel, stoel and bed take de; huis takes het. Roughly three quarters of nouns are de-words, but frequency is not a rule. Compounds follow their last element, and every diminutive is het. Adjectives add -e after de/het or a possessive: het grote huis, mijn grote huis — but een groot huis has no -e.
pattern.linguist_note: Dutch merged the old masculine and feminine genders into a common gender (de) while keeping the neuter (het). The resulting system has two articles but no noun case.
pattern.trap_note: Do not choose de or het from the object's meaning or sex. A table is not feminine and a house is not neuter because of what they are; the word carries the article.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (De & Het: Gender Without Case):
exercises.target_answer: de, het, de tafel, de stoel, het bed, het huis
exercises.meaning: the (common gender), it; the (neuter), table, chair, bed, house
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "De & Het: Gender Without Case": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “The table is big.”?
exercises.explanation: “De tafel is groot.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “De & Het: Gender Without Case”.

cues: The pattern: Read the word, not the meaning
It means: The house is small.
exercises.explanation: “Het huis is klein.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Read the word, not the meaning.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not choose de or het from the object's meaning or sex. A table is not feminine and a house is not neuter because of what they are; the word carries the article.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “De stoel is oud.” is word-for-word “The chair is old.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Read the word, not the meaning.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: The big house is old.
exercises.explanation: “Het grote huis is oud.” reuses only material taught in “De & Het: Gender Without Case” — Read the word, not the meaning.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Het grote huis is oud.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Read the word, not the meaning.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “The book is on the table.”
twist.target_answer: Het boek is op de tafel.
twist.explanation: The prepositional phrase keeps de before tafel; het belongs to boek.

summary.outcome: Use de and het as lexical articles, add adjective -e after a definite phrase, and stop looking for case endings.
summary.takeaway: Dutch gender is a two-way article system with no noun case — smaller than German, not random.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: De/Het Decoder.

de.etymology_derivation: The common-gender article; roughly three quarters of Dutch nouns take it.

het.etymology_derivation: The neuter pronoun and article are the same little word; English split it into it and the.

tafel.etymology_derivation: Latin tabula gave English table and Dutch tafel.

stoel.etymology_derivation: English stool and Dutch stoel are the same word; Dutch narrowed it to chair.

bed.etymology_derivation: English bed and Dutch bed are direct twins.

huis.etymology_derivation: English house and Dutch huis are the same word; ui answers to ou.

sch_sh.name: The SCH Bridge
sch_sh.phonetic_rule: English /ʃ/ (sh) corresponds to Dutch /sx/ (sch): ship → schip, shoe → schoen, sheep → schaap.
sch_sh.historical_linguistics: West Germanic *sk stayed a sk-like cluster in Dutch, spelled sch, while English palatalised it to sh.
sch_sh.philological_note: Dutch sch is not English sh; the ch is a voiceless velar fricative. School is a Latin loan shared by both languages.

th_d.name: The TH → D Bridge
th_d.phonetic_rule: English th corresponds to Dutch d: brother → broeder, three → drie, think → denken, thank → danken.
th_d.historical_linguistics: The Germanic dental fricative hardened to a stop in Dutch and German; English kept the fricative.
th_d.philological_note: Weather/weer is cognate but Dutch lost the d, so it is not a th↔d example. Loans such as theater keep t.

f_v.name: The F → V Bridge
f_v.phonetic_rule: English f often corresponds to Dutch v: father → vader, foot → voet, fish → vis.
f_v.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic f to v in many positions; English kept the voiceless consonant.
f_v.philological_note: Northern Dutch often devoices v to [f], especially in vr-/vl- clusters and word-finally; the spelling keeps the historical v.

s_z.name: The S → Z Bridge
s_z.phonetic_rule: English s often corresponds to Dutch z: sun → zon, sea → zee, salt → zout.
s_z.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic s before vowels; English kept s.
s_z.philological_note: Clusters sn/sm/sl keep s (sneeuw, smal, slapen); loans such as school and straat also keep s.

gh_ch.name: The GH → CH Bridge
gh_ch.phonetic_rule: English gh corresponds to Dutch ch: night → nacht, light → licht, right → recht, eight → acht.
gh_ch.historical_linguistics: English gh and Dutch ch descend from a shared velar fricative; English vocalised or lost it, Dutch kept it.
gh_ch.philological_note: Dutch g is the voiced partner of ch. The two are different sounds, not spelling variants.

vowel_ij.name: The IJ Bridge
vowel_ij.phonetic_rule: Dutch ij is /ɛi/ and often answers to English i/y: ice → ijs, wine → wijn, five → vijf.
vowel_ij.historical_linguistics: The digraph ij spells a Dutch diphthong; English orthography kept a different vowel from the same Germanic stock.
vowel_ij.philological_note: IJ is two letters but one sound. It is not English /aɪ/.

vowel_ui.name: The UI Bridge
vowel_ui.phonetic_rule: Dutch ui is /œy/ and often answers to English ou/ow: house → huis, mouse → muis, out → uit.
vowel_ui.historical_linguistics: Dutch ui spells a front rounded diphthong with no close English equivalent; the English spelling twin is a memory hook.
vowel_ui.philological_note: Do not pronounce ui as two English beats; it is one gliding vowel.

vowel_oe.name: The OE Bridge
vowel_oe.phonetic_rule: Dutch oe is /u/ and often answers to English oo/u in spelling: book → boek, foot → voet, good → goed.
vowel_oe.historical_linguistics: The Dutch digraph oe spells a long /u/; English oo spells several different vowels, so this is a spelling/cognacy bridge.
vowel_oe.philological_note: Dutch oe is /u/, not the /ʊ/ of English book. Read the Dutch spelling and use the Dutch sound.

g_y.name: The G / Y Bridge
g_y.phonetic_rule: English g and some y words correspond to voiced Dutch g: gold → goud, good → goed, yellow → geel.
g_y.historical_linguistics: Dutch kept a velar fricative where English kept a stop or palatalised to y. English year/jaar is y↔j, not y↔g.
g_y.philological_note: Dutch g is a fricative, never the English stop in 'good'.
